name: Mako
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: Rosés Labrada, Jorge Emilio. 2015. The Mako language: Vitality, Grammar and Classification. PhD dissertation, University of Western Ontario / Université Lumière-Lyon 2. xxix+560 pp. Open access:https://uwo.scholaris.ca/items/4e02229e-cc93-4672-b94e-b38e6330b454(handle 20.500.14721/35789).
catalog_locator: §4.3 'Stress', pp. 202-203; restated §4.5 'Conclusions', p. 205; chapter-4 intro, p. 161 ('word-level stress'); §4.1 cross-reference, p. 170
catalog_quote: Stress in Mako is word-final. Figure 46, Figure 47, and Figure 48 show both the pitch (in blue) and intensity (in yellow) contours for a two-syllable word, a three-syllable word and a five-syllable word. As can be seen in the first two figures below, both the pitch and the intensity contours correspond to one another and both reach their maximum value on the last syllable. In Figure 48, the pitch contour peaks on the fourth (from the right) syllable while the intensity contour remains as word final. It could be that in this case the speaker is exploiting both pitch and intensity to distinguish between primary and secondary stress but more research is needed in this area. ... Stress is in principle non-contrastive but one of my consultants affirms that there is a difference between [ˈdakɨ] and [daˈkɨ]; the first word would mean ‘already’ ‘enough!’ and the second one would mean ‘no’. However, I do not hear a contrastive difference in this (supposedly) minimal pair; an acoustic analysis would aid to elucidate this question. ... [§4.5] I have also shown that stress in Mako is word-final and that the language’s syllable structure is (C)V. Stress and syllable structure are two areas where further research is likely to prove fruitful.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the final syllable of the word (pitch peak and intensity peak coincide on the last syllable in 2- and 3-syllable words; intensity peak remains final in a 5-syllable word). Stress is treated as non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not analysed; in the 5-syllable word [ɨʦɨdemida] the pitch peak sits on the 4th syllable from the right while intensity is final, which the author suggests may reflect a primary/secondary stress distinction; 'more research is needed'.
new_statements.exceptions: One consultant claims a minimal pair [ˈdakɨ] 'already; enough!' vs [daˈkɨ] 'no'; the author does not hear the contrast and calls for acoustic analysis. Stress is 'in principle non-contrastive'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; based on isolated citation-form words (2, 3 and 5 syllables) with pitch/intensity traces; also holds for conjugated verb forms with past suffix /tə/ (§4.1, Figure 14). Syllable structure (C)V, so weight plays no role. Author flags stress as needing further research.
new_statements.identity_note: The dissertation describes Mako (also spelled Maco; self-designation reported as Wirö/Jojodö in the text) of the Ventuari River area, Amazonas state, Venezuela — same variety as Glottolog maco1239 / ISO wpc. The earlier scan marked the source unreachable because ir.lib.uwo.ca now redirects; the repository migrated to uwo.scholaris.ca (handle 20.500.14721/35789), where the full PDF is open access.

sources.note: SAPhon codes tone in each inventory's 'Suprasegmental' field (checked: Bora shows 'Tone' there); for Mako the field reads 'None', i.e. the database records no tone and no other contrastive suprasegmental feature (no contrastive stress, no nasal harmony) for Mako, secondhand from Rosés Labrada (2015). Inventory otherwise: /pʰ tʰ ʔb ʔd ʔdʒ p t ts tʃ k kʷ ʔ b d dʒ hʷ h m n w ʔw l/, vowels /i ɨ u e o a/ each with a nasal counterpart; note on a marginal /ə/ in the past-tense suffix.
